result.white_space: Nobody I found runs the specific thing proposed: a paid supply-side network of trade professionals (inspectors, plumbers, water-heater installers) who photograph the service entry under a fixed protocol, with vision-AI classification, tamper-evident geo-verification, human QA, and export to state inventory formats, sold to utilities per verified line. Players fall into four groups. (1) Predictive modelers (BlueConduit, VODA.ai) reduce digs statistically but still need ground-truth field samples, and Texas does not accept predictive modeling for official inventories. (2) Customer self-ID portals (Trinnex leadCAST, Esri Survey123, Cognito Forms) collect photos and reach only the 10-25% of owners who respond, and absentee landlords and LLCs almost never do. (3) Hardware probes (Electro Scan, Echologics) need a utility crew at each line. (4) Door-to-door inspection programs (RCAP, engineering firms) are staffed centrally and slowly. The unserved wedge is professional-grade evidence for the non-responding, owner-absent lines at about $30-60 per line, collected by people already inside the building. Two sub-gaps stand out: states that reject modeling but accept documented visual verification, and small or mid-size utilities with no field crews. Caveats: (a) my WebSearch budget ran out after 4 searches, so Crunchbase, YC, Product Hunt and GitHub sweeps were not done and a stealth or very early startup in this niche could exist; (b) the search snippet says physical identification methods 'must be conducted or overseen by water system personnel' (state-dependent), so third-party photos may only count as self-ID-grade evidence unless the utility or state accepts contractor verification; (c) the idea's own note that regulatory details are from memory still applies; (d) per-utility supply is limited to home sales and water-heater swaps, so density per utility could be slow; (e) inspectors may resist liability for calling a pipe lead (my recollection, unverified); (f) Trinnex or Esri could add a 'contractor submission' role cheaply.
result.evidence_of_demand: Moderate to strong for the problem, and only indirect for this specific mechanism. (1) Utilities already pay households to submit pipe photos. Durham offers a $30 water-bill credit for a verified self-ID with photos, which validates the incentive price point and the photo-as-evidence approach (https://www.durhamnc.gov/5184/Water-Service-Line-Inventory-and-Verific). The same page tells residents to check their home-inspection report because 'the home inspector may have identified your service line material and included a photo', so inspector photos are already used ad hoc but nobody pays for them. (2) Verification cost and time pain are quantified by a vendor: BlueConduit claims physical verification takes 3-10+ years and that a system with 5,000 unknowns can save over $4.5M and 5 years, which implies roughly $900 per unknown by digging (https://blueconduit.com/lsl-unknown-management/). (3) Utilities buy verification technology. Rock Hill, SC purchased two Swordfish units and targeted about 14,000 homes (https://trenchlesstechnology.com/identifying-water-service-line-pipe-materials-using-machine-intelligent-technology/), and Detroit's use of BlueConduit avoided an estimated $380M of excavation (https://news.bloomberglaw.com/environment-and-energy/ai-speeds-cities-lead-pipe-search-with-epa-deadline-weeks-away). (4) Regulatory pressure and the modeling gap: the EPA's October 2024 LCRI requires identifying and replacing lead pipes within 10 years (https://www.epa.gov/ground-water-and-drinking-water/lead-and-copper-rule-improvements). Bloomberg Law reports many systems filed substantial 'unknown' counts, the NRDC calls it a fundamental problem, and Texas does not accept predictive modeling for official inventories, which forces physical or visual verification. (5) Funding tie-in: BIL provides $15B for LSL replacement through state revolving funds, and BlueConduit notes systems win funding most often when they minimize unknowns first (https://blueconduit.com/post/what-funding-is-available-for-replacing-privately-owned-lead-service-lines/). Not found: any RFP, forum thread or purchase order for per-line paid third-party photo verification, or any home inspector asking to be paid for this. That demand is unproven.
result.sharper_angle: Do not lead with a consumer-facing inspector bounty marketplace, where free Esri and Survey123 forms and leadCAST-style portals with a $30 credit already cover the customer-photo layer. Position as the verification-grade evidence and field-sampling layer that plugs into the tools utilities and consultants already use. Three moves. (1) Sell to the predictive modelers and engineering firms first (BlueConduit, VODA.ai, Stantec, Hazen-type consultants). Their models require 'representative field investigations' and ground-truth samples, and states like Texas require physical verification. Offer a per-line, tamper-evident, professionally collected photo sample at a fraction of potholing cost, so you are the channel partner rather than a competitor with a 6-12 month municipal sales cycle. (2) Replace recruit-and-pay-each-inspector with distribution through chokepoints that already put a trade professional next to the pipe. That means embedding the 3-photo protocol as a module in home-inspection report software, and as a water-heater or plumbing-permit closeout requirement that utilities or cities can mandate for near-zero bounty. Target absentee-landlord and LLC-owned rentals through rental registration and inspection programs, the cohort self-ID portals cannot reach. (3) Start in one state that explicitly accepts documented contractor or visual verification and rejects pure modeling. Get a written acceptance letter from the state drinking-water program before selling anything, and publish potholed ground-truth accuracy on the first 200 lines. Integrate outputs into Esri and leadCAST rather than replacing them. Before building, confirm with 3-5 state programs whether third-party photo verification can reclassify an 'unknown' line to non-lead or lead, and with 10 inspectors whether they will accept the liability and effort for $15-25 per line.

result.white_space: Among the products I could find, none sells the specific signal in this idea: an external-behavior signal (a floored VIN vanishing from the dealer site or marketplaces) checked against the lender's own payoff ledger on a running clock, with a ranked daily queue. Existing offerings cover other things. Physical or photo audits (CSI, LotCount, SBS Digital Audit, Netresult) are periodic and dealer-cooperative. Platforms (Vero, Solifi, Alfa, SBS servicing) analyze the lender's own payment and title data. Bank-data tools (Plaid-style) watch dealer cash. DRN covers location. The unserved wedge is mid-size and small lenders that lack data-science teams: independent floorplan companies, credit unions and community banks with dealer lines, and third-party audit firms that need risk-based audit targeting. It is strongest for used-car and buy-here-pay-here dealers, where captives' retail-delivery reports do not exist. Caveats that shrink the white space: (1) captives see retail deliveries within days and can build the signal in-house, and the SAS paper suggests at least one lender did; (2) Vero, SBS and Cox/NextGear could bolt on the signal; (3) a listing that disappears is a noisy signal (wholesaled, transferred, in recon, or the dealer never lists), so precision must be proven; (4) marketplace scraping has terms-of-service risk, so a licensed feed such as MarketCheck is likely needed.
result.evidence_of_demand: Strong evidence that the problem is real and that lenders spend on adjacent controls. None found that anyone pays for this exact signal. (1) The Sky Auto Mall case: Ford Credit and Stellantis Financial sued over floorplan fraud and out-of-trust sales. Stellantis claims more than $12.3M and about $1.4M in unreturned sale proceeds. Ford claims $6.6M. Ford found 81 double-financed units only after Stellantis tipped it off and it compared lists. The dealer group then filed for bankruptcy. Sources: https://www.carscoops.com/2026/03/iowa-stellantis-ford-dealer/ , https://www.autonews.com/retail/an-stellantis-ford-captives-sue-iowa-dealership-out-of-trust-0317/ (page returned 403; seen only in search results), https://www.autofinancenews.net/allposts/risk-management/sky-auto-mall-owners-file-for-bankruptcy-amid-18m-floorplan-fraud-lawsuits/ (page returned 403; seen only in search results). Note that the fraud was mainly double-flooring, which listing disappearance would not catch. Only the sold-without-payoff part fits the idea. (2) Vendors are marketing directly at this pain. Vero published a floorplan fraud series (April 2026) that says physical audits are snapshots, that 10 to 15% of inventory turns between 30 to 45 day audit cycles, and that lenders lack cross-lender visibility. Sources: https://www.vero-technologies.com/news/the-hidden-mechanics-behind-double-flooring-what-recent-dealership-fraud-stories-actually-show and https://www.vero-technologies.com/news/how-a-single-fraud-story-exposed-a-systemic-floorplan-blind-spot . (3) Spend on audit workarounds is large. SBS reports more than 100,000 digital audits in the US by end 2025, per https://www.vero-technologies.com/news/ai-in-wholesale-finance-whats-actually-happening-on-the-ground , which also says dealer-services teams at banks want to 'automate audit triage and SOT reporting'. A March 2026 Young & Associates piece says audits are tedious, that discrepancies found after weeks or months raise loss severity, and describes a double-floored dealer found by audit: https://www.younginc.com/blog/the-importance-of-floor-plan-audits-for-lending-institutions/ . MOBI says lenders hold reserves because audits are infrequent, and a consortium including Ford Credit, GM Financial and Stellantis piloted automated audit tech: https://dlt.mobi/dfa/ . (4) The 'audit-triage' framing is supported, but I found no RFPs, pricing pages or forum posts showing lenders paying $15 to $30 per dealer per month for listing-based monitoring. That price point is unvalidated. Research limits: the web-search budget ran out after 4 searches, and several pages (LotCount, AFC, SAS paper, Solifi) could not be fetched. I did not check Crunchbase, YC or Product Hunt, and GitHub repository searches for open-source tools returned nothing.
result.sharper_angle: Do not sell a standalone 'radar' dashboard. Sell it as an audit-targeting and triage layer that turns the listing-disappearance-plus-missing-payoff signal into a daily ranked list of specific VINs to verify within 24 to 48 hours. Sell it through channels that already own the lender relationship: (a) as a signal module or partner integration for the audit vendors and platforms (SBS Digital Audit, LotCount, CSI, Vero, Solifi), which turns the platforms from likely competitors into distributors, and (b) direct to independent floorplan lenders, credit unions and community banks with used-car and BHPH dealers, where there are no captive retail-delivery reports and no data-science team. Price per verified catch or per audit-hour saved, not a flat $20 per dealer. The proof to lead with is a backtest showing what share of already-confirmed SOT cases the signal flagged, and the false-positive rate, since delisting is noisy. Then add the piece no single-lender tool has: a cross-lender check that flags a VIN floored with two lenders while still publicly listed. Vero itself names single-lender visibility as the blind spot. Use a licensed listing feed such as MarketCheck to avoid scraping and terms-of-service risk. Treat the dealer-facing 'fix your unpaid VINs' view and the contracts-in-transit tracker as a later upsell, not the wedge. Before building, spend two weeks re-running the incumbent check with unrestricted search (Crunchbase, YC, Product Hunt, Cox/NextGear and AFC/OPENLANE product pages) and interview five lender risk or audit heads to confirm the signal would change their audit order.

result.white_space:
Caveat first: the WebSearch budget (200 of 200) was already spent when I started, so I ran zero searches. I did direct fetches of about 15 vendor and agency pages, plus GitHub repo searches. Nothing here rules out a direct competitor. The biggest gap is that I could not identify the third-party collateral-inspection firms that lenders already pay for cattle counts, or any startup selling vet-verified herd inventory to lenders. Do not treat 'gap' as 'open'.

What the direct fetches showed: none of the herd-software, EID, tracking or verification vendors I checked advertise a lender-facing 'independent count' product. The vendors were CattleMax, AgriWebb, IMI Global/WFCF, Ceres Tag, Halter, HerdDogg and Gallagher. Merck/Vence returned 403, so I could not check it. Every one of them is a producer-side management or supply-chain tool. GitHub searches turned up no open-source lender-verification tool, only hobby herd apps.

The unserved wedge is a lender-mandated, third-party-attested herd inventory built as a covenant workflow. It would cover the vet-signed chute-side count, a portfolio dashboard, and year-over-year anomaly flags such as head count down, pregnancy rate down, or tags missing versus last year.

Structural weaknesses to be skeptical of:
- Adverse selection: 'borrower-initiated' verification means fraudulent borrowers never opt in. The product only works if lenders make it a loan condition.
- Coverage: a preg-check only counts animals brought to the chute that day, not cattle on other leases or sold or double-pledged since. It does not prove ownership or lien priority.
- Vet liability and willingness: vets may refuse to sign anything that reads as a collateral audit.
- Economics: $2-3/head split 50/50 leaves the vet about $1-1.50/head on top of a preg-check fee that is already several dollars.
- Entry by an existing vendor: IMI Global (WFCF) or Merck/Allflex could add this as a feature.
result.evidence_of_demand: None verified this session, because I could not run searches. Two specific claims in the idea are unconfirmed: the '2026 roughly $9.4M fraud, including a $2.8M loan against 850 head', and the Nov 2024 federal EID rule. The EID claim is consistent with my prior knowledge but my APHIS fetch returned 404 (https://www.aphis.usda.gov/livestock-poultry-disease/traceability/cattle). The Eastern Livestock Wikipedia fetch also returned 404. The OCC Agricultural Lending handbook PDF (https://www.occ.gov/publications-and-resources/publications/comptrollers-handbook/files/agricultural-lending/pub-ch-agricultural-lending.pdf) fetched but did not extract as readable text. Farm Credit's homepage (https://www.farmcredit.com/) shows no verification tooling. It is background knowledge, not something I confirmed here, that lenders already do collateral inspections and that historic cattle-collateral frauds such as Eastern Livestock (2010) exist. That points to real spend on manual workarounds, but the founder should confirm it with lender interviews. No RFPs, forum complaints or paid-service pricing were found.
result.kill_reason: n/a. Nothing found shows a dominant or crowded direct competitor. The evidence is thin because no web searches were possible, so this is a provisional not-killed verdict pending a proper competitor search.
result.sharper_angle: Skip the vet-as-attestor framing and sell to the lender as a covenant-compliance tool. Give the loan officer an 'inventory attestation' workflow they attach to the loan agreement, with three parts. (1) Accept attestations from any credible chute-side handler (vet, brand inspector, sale-barn or feedyard records, EID reader logs), not only vets, so a vet's reluctance does not block the product. (2) Reconcile each attestation against independent sources: the lender's prior-year counts, sale-barn and movement records, and EID or CVI data. The output is a reconciled 'expected vs. attested head' variance flag, which is what catches fraud. (3) Track the lien and ownership side (UCC and brand records) next to the count. Start with a single community-bank or Farm Credit association pilot that makes it a condition on new bred-heifer and operating-line loans. Have the bank pay, priced per loan or per portfolio, to avoid the 'honest borrower must opt in' adverse-selection trap. Before building, run 10-15 lender and vet interviews and a proper search for existing third-party inspection vendors. Also test whether IMI Global/WFCF (Beef Passport) or a big EID vendor would white-label this.

result.white_space:
Across this session's research I found no direct competitor selling packaged, hardware-validated large-load dynamic models (PSS/E plus EMT) with ride-through study reports and certification letters for GPU-cluster, PSU and UPS stacks. Nobody was seen selling OEM-level type-test certification for power shelves and UPS platforms. Adjacent players cover only pieces: HIL tools (Typhoon HIL, OPAL-RT), generic EMT consultancies, EPRI's flexibility consortium, workload-flex software (Emerald AI), and simulation software vendors with no data center library shown.

Three structural threats need answers:
1. Regulators and EPRI or NERC may publish free generic composite or EMT models, which commoditizes the model library.
2. OEMs (UPS, PSU, NVIDIA) own the confidential control details and may ship their own models.
3. Per-project EMT consulting already exists and is not verified either way for large loads.

The defensible white space is independent, hardware-validated, ISO-acceptable model packages and compliance evidence for the 25-500 MW neocloud and colo developers who lack in-house power simulators. It would be reused across sites through OEM platform type tests, not sold as bespoke studies.

Research limits: the WebSearch budget (200 calls) was exhausted before this task began, so competitor discovery relied on direct page fetches and GitHub search. Startup databases (Crunchbase, YC, Product Hunt), news, and NERC or EPRI publication pages were not checked. Several NERC, EPRI and PJM URLs returned 404 or empty content. Treat the 'no direct competitor' finding as moderate-confidence. Verify manually against NERC LLTF outputs, EPRI data center model reports, and WECC or ERCOT model requirements before committing.
result.evidence_of_demand:
Regulatory forcing functions are confirmed on ERCOT's own pages:
- ERCOT NOGRR282 (Large Computational Load Ride-Through Requirements) was approved by the PUCT on July 9, 2026 and took effect August 1, 2026. It sets frequency and voltage ride-through requirements for data centers. https://www.ercot.com/mktrules/issues/NOGRR282 . The summary page did not disclose thresholds, model-submission or test/attestation requirements, so how compliance is verified is unconfirmed.
- ERCOT PGRR115 creates a Large Load Interconnection Study process for loads of 25 MW or more, requires stability assessments before energization, and adds large loads to the Network Operations Model. Approved by the PUCT 5/15/2025, effective 11/3/2025 and 12/15/2025. https://www.ercot.com/mktrules/issues/PGRR115
- ERCOT NPRR1234 sets interconnection standards for loads of 75 MW or more, modeling standards for loads of 25 MW or more, and subsynchronous oscillation requirements for large loads. Effective 12/15/2025. https://www.ercot.com/mktrules/issues/NPRR1234
- ERCOT's Large Load Working Group is building a batch study process for large load interconnections. https://www.ercot.com/committees/tac/llwg

Technical and market signals:
- Hyperscalers publicly describe GPU power swings that could align with grid infrastructure frequencies and are building in-house simulators. https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.14318
- Investors value adjacent data-center-grid software highly: Emerald AI raised a $150M Series A at a $1.05B valuation in Aug 2026. https://www.emeraldai.co/
- Typhoon HIL sells data center HIL validation to OEMs and operators, which shows existing spend on testing. https://www.typhoon-hil.com/solutions/grid-modernization/data-centers/

Not found or not verified:
- No RFPs, price points, or forum complaints showing willingness to pay $75-300k per project.
- The NERC incident review of the 1.5 GW Northern Virginia trip and NERC Large Loads Task Force pages (fetched URLs 404'd or returned no content) were not confirmed here. The idea's own claims about them are unverified by this research.
- Evidence is regulatory demand, not proven paid demand.
result.sharper_angle:
Drop 'the model library is the moat', because generic models will likely be published free by NERC, EPRI, WECC or ISOs and OEMs own their control details. Reframe as an independent large-load type-test and compliance-evidence service, the analogue of inverter type-certification (IEEE 2800 / UL 1741 for generators). Three moves:
1. Start Texas-first, as 'ERCOT LCL ride-through readiness'. NOGRR282 took effect August 1, 2026, and PGRR115 and NPRR1234 already require studies and models for 25 MW and larger sites. Sell fixed-scope packages to neoclouds, colo developers and their EPCs that have no in-house power simulators, unlike Microsoft. Each package is a gap analysis, then an ISO-acceptable PSS/E plus EMT model, a ride-through study, and a compliance file.
2. Get the moat from confidential, NDA-protected, HIL-validated models of specific UPS and power-shelf platforms. Get the certification and test fees from those OEMs (Vertiv, Eaton, Schneider, power-shelf makers), so one platform test is reused across many sites.
3. Partner with Typhoon HIL or OPAL-RT and a university lab instead of competing with them. Position against Emerald AI as compliance evidence for the fast-ramping fixed load, not workload flexibility.

Before committing, verify what NOGRR282 requires for compliance evidence, since a model-and-test requirement is what makes this sellable, and check EPRI and NERC for free reference models.

result.white_space:
No company found that bundles the four pieces (workfile custody plus subpoena and board-inquiry response, tail, local-knowledge capture, direct-lender client handoff to a supervised successor). Searches for retiring-appraiser succession services, workfile custodian services, and appraiser practice brokers returned only DIY articles from WorkingRE, McKissock, Appraisal Today and NAR.

Specific white space that survives:
(1) Third-party workfile custody and retrieval (agent-of-record for subpoenas and board requests) for retired or deceased appraisers. USPAP requires retention and retrievability for 5+ years, with regulators able to act later, and no dedicated vendor was found. Software vendors and cloud storage only store files, and nobody answers a subpoena for you.
(2) Local, rural or community-lender-funded succession. Aloft, Valligent and Solidifi are national or AMC-centric, not local continuity for a single county.
(3) The retiree-as-mentor stipend and earn-out structure, which none of the trainee programs use.

Specific weaknesses in the idea:
(a) The 'tail is frightening and costly' pain is largely solved for long-tenured appraisers by free LIA and OREP retirement tails. The paid pain is limited to those with short E&O tenure, gaps, or sub-5-year policies. Tail brokerage commissions are therefore thin.
(b) Fee-splitting and finder's-fee rules. Minnesota (82B.20) bans commission-splitting, rebates and finder's fees with appraisers, and other states have similar rules. An earn-out on inherited client revenue and a 20-30% take on trainee fees may be illegal in some states unless structured as a sale of a business or as employment.
(c) Supervisor-of-record is not passive. State rules limit trainee counts (Aloft cites 3 per supervisor), require certification in good standing and the supervisor's own E&O, and make the supervisor take full responsibility. A retiree who stays on as supervisor is not really retired and keeps license, CE and E&O costs.
(d) Client transferability is weak. Appraisal Today notes practices under $200K are 'buying a job', and residential lender relationships are 'fickle'. Most practices sell at 0.33-0.5x revenue with seller financing, and AMC-dependent revenue is not transferable.
(e) Pipeline substitutes are growing: PAREA, AXIS/CRN trainee-inspection reform, Valligent and Aloft paying supervisors.
result.evidence_of_demand:
Demand for exit is strong. Demand to PAY for this bundle is not proven, and I found no example of a retiree paying for workfile custody or a succession service.

Evidence the exit wave is real:
- WorkingRE 2026 Appraiser Survey: 31% plan to leave within 3 years, about 50% within 5 years, 57% of active appraisers are over 60, first-time test takers down 70% since 2009 (4,790 to 1,421 in 2025), and only 820 passed in 2025. https://www.workingre.com/2026-appraiser-survey-state-of-the-profession/
- Workforce fell from about 92,000 in 2016 to about 65,000 in June 2025. https://www.workingre.com/the-decline-of-appraisers/
- UAD 3.6 mandatory Nov 2, 2026, with commentators saying some veterans will exit rather than retool. https://www.mckissock.com/blog/appraisal/the-future-is-now-fannie-mae-and-freddie-mac-announce-uad-3-6-implementation-timeline-and-policy-changes/ and https://remdamno557947.substack.com/p/the-ones-who-are-leaving-and-the
- Only 16% of appraisers are willing to train, and lack of compensation is the top reason. https://nationalmortgageprofessional.com/news/lending-hand-appraiser-trainees
- Regulator and lender pressure: EO 14393 (Mar 13, 2026) directs simplified appraiser qualifications and more alternative valuation. https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2026/03/18/2026-05384/promoting-access-to-mortgage-credit. AQB second exposure draft (June 22, 2026) proposes dropping the college requirements. https://appraisaltoday.com/2026/06/25/aqb-exposure-draft-removes-college-degree-requirement/. Reported comment deadlines conflict (Aug 30 vs July 27). ABA Banking Journal and CSBS document rural appraiser shortages. https://bankingjournal.aba.com/2026/06/effective-strategies-for-managing-an-appraiser-shortage/
- USPAP retention and retrievability duties survive retirement; guidance says keep files longer than the minimum because regulators can act after it lapses. https://www.mckissock.com/appraisal/uspap/understanding-uspap/uspap-record-keeping-rule/ and https://memberships.theappraisercoach.com/blog/workfiles-beyond-retirement
- Forum activity about retirement, tail and workfile worries. https://appraisersforum.com/forums/threads/retiring-from-appraisal-tail-end-coverage.240529/page-4
- Practices do sell, at 0.25-1.4x revenue (mostly 0.33-0.5x, seller-financed, 6-12 month transition). https://appraisaltoday.com/biz-tips/can-you-sell-your-appraisal-business/

Evidence against or missing:
- Free tail from LIA and OREP for eligible veterans, as noted in the competitors.
- Nothing found showing that retirees pay for custody, that credit unions pay for 'coverage guarantees', or that trainee-farm supervisor fees are accepted.
- Retirees' stated alternatives are DIY: keep the files, keep the tail, let the license lapse. Also, about 15% of residential appraisers are already not actively practicing (ABA Banking Journal).
result.sharper_angle:
Drop the trainee farm, the earn-out and the tail brokerage, and narrow to the one piece nobody serves. Make it a records-custodian and regulatory-response service for retired and deceased appraisers, sold through the channels that already reach them.

What it is: a third-party workfile custodian and agent-of-record that stores the files, holds retrievability under USPAP, and answers subpoenas and board requests on the retiree's behalf. Price it at about $29/month or a one-time lifetime fee, and offer an estate and heirs version.

Why this wedge:
- Free LIA and OREP retirement tails already cover the money risk but do not preserve or produce the workfile, which is the main defense in a claim.
- E&O carriers, the Appraisal Institute, state boards and estates have an incentive to fund it as a loss-control benefit. That gives a distribution channel and avoids selling to 58-year-olds one by one.
- It avoids fee-splitting law and supervisor-licensing problems entirely.

Wedge 2, only after custody has traction: a lender-funded 'local coverage continuity' program for rural community banks and credit unions. The retiree is paid a fixed mentor or reviewer fee, not a percentage of the successor's revenue, to hand a named successor (an existing trainee or certified appraiser) the local-knowledge playbook and direct-client introductions. This keeps out of Aloft's and Valligent's national AMC-style lane by staying single-county and bank-sponsored.

Before building, validate with 20 retiring appraisers on willingness to pay for custody, and get one E&O administrator (LIA or OREP) to say they would refer or co-brand. If neither is true, the idea collapses to a free feature."

competitors.name: Site Selection Group and other site-selection consultants (Cushman & Wakefield, BLS Strategies)
competitors.what_they_do: Custom advisory work that says power is now 'the starting point' and tells clients to evaluate existing service, utilisation and incremental capacity. No productised building database was described in the article. The firms could add this as a service line, or become customers.
competitors.scale_or_funding: Established consultancies

competitors.name: Property Condition Assessment and electrical inspection firms
competitors.what_they_do: Commodity alternative. An ASTM E2018 PCA already has to state service ampacity, voltage and phase, and buyers can hire a commercial electrician pre-purchase. This is the workaround customers use today; it is bespoke, unscored and not tied to permits or a database.
competitors.scale_or_funding: Fragmented local engineering and inspection firms

result.white_space: Nobody I found productises a building-level, physically verified 'inside-the-fence' record for dead Midwest plants. That record would cover the electrician-verified main service size, voltage, gear age and nameplates, spare capacity, slab and crane-rail condition, the state of the existing air and wastewater permits, and a utility will-serve letter, all in a scored, comparable format sold before the deal. The funded players (LandGate, Enverus, GridCARE, Paces) work at the substation and grid level and are aimed at data centers. Utility and state databases (JobsOhio, AEP, FirstEnergy, ZoomProspector) verify sites and utility service, not building gear or permit status. Scout and Brownfield.ai are the closest competitors, but they look desktop- and network-led with no per-building inspection, and I found no evidence they carry electrician-verified data. The genuine gap is a trusted, standardised, seller-commissioned building electrical and permit record, not the parcel-scoring layer, which is already crowded and funded. The idea's weaker points: the Ohio permit-transferability wedge is thin (see evidence), and it is unproven that brokers will pay $1.5k-$3.5k.
result.evidence_of_demand:
Partial evidence only. I found no RFPs, forum threads or existing broker spend on this specific product.

Supporting evidence:
- Power is now a lead site-selection criterion. Site Selection Group says 'power availability, upgrade timelines, and utility costs have become the starting point' for manufacturers (https://info.siteselectiongroup.com/blog/why-power-availability-is-altering-manufacturing-site-selection). Similar pieces: Voit (https://voitco.com/access-to-power-the-new-priority-for-industrial-site-selection/), Link Logistics (https://www.linklogistics.com/news-insights/industry-expertise/power-capacity-in-warehouse-site-selection/), JLL (https://www.jll.com/en-us/newsroom/power-availability-becoming-key-driver-of-cre-value), and Utility Dive on power-ready facilities (https://www.utilitydive.com/news/big-power-ready-facilities-key-as-occupiers-drive-industrial-market-improv/822244/).
- Equipment lead times are long. Large transformers average about 128 weeks (https://syaala.com/blog/transformer-lead-times-2026). Switchgear runs about 44 weeks on average and 90+ in some markets (https://usevawn.com/resources/electrical-equipment-lead-times/).
- Undersized service is a common post-lease surprise, with upgrades of about 3-9 months and $50k-$500k+ (WareCRE-style industrial spec guidance, https://warecre.com/cre-insights/industrial-101/loading-docks-ceiling-heights-and-power-requirements-understanding-industrial-property-specs/; attribution is from a search snippet and not verified).
- Customers already pay for power-availability reports. SCE sells an Engineering Analysis Report for about $3,000 covering power availability and time to build infrastructure (https://www.inboundlogistics.com/articles/utilities-and-site-selection-a-powerful-partnership/). The price sits inside your $1.5k-$3.5k band, but it is a utility-issued report, not a broker-paid one.
- Investors are paying for the adjacent data layer: GridCARE's $64M Series A (https://www.latitudemedia.com/news/gridcare-raises-oversubscribed-64-million-series-a/) and Paces' $11M Series A.
- Data centers are competing for existing energized industrial shells. Akron's former Goodyear plant now runs about 150 MW (https://signalakron.org/where-7-data-centers-operate-in-summit-county-and-why-it-matters/). TeraWulf and Anthropic signed a $19B lease on a shuttered aluminum plant (https://www.constructionaibrief.com/posts/2026-07-08-terawulf-anthropic-brownfield-aluminum-plant-data-center). Host Digital Infrastructure has a 45+ MW converted facility (https://www.globenewswire.com/news-release/2026/09/03/3356181/0/en/the-scarcest-thing-in-the-ai-buildout-is-a-site-that-already-has-power.html). Bisnow: https://www.bisnow.com/national/news/data-center/brownfield-data-centers-109798.

Counter-evidence:
- The 2026 Reshoring Initiative survey coverage I retrieved names workforce (66% rate technician hiring very difficult or crisis) and policy uncertainty (57% of OEMs) as the main challenges, and does not mention power or permitting (https://www.qualitymag.com/articles/99902-new-survey-us-reshoring-momentum-builds-despite-policy-and-workforce-challenges). The founder's claim that reshorers lose a year to power and permits is not backed by that survey.
- Ohio EPA guidance says an ownership transfer needs only a notification letter within 30 days, and no permit modification unless the new owner requests one (https://epa.ohio.gov/static/Portals/27/eBusinessCenter/Agency/DAPC/GUIDANCE_tranownership.doc). Idle facilities can keep permits if fees and reports stay current. That makes 'transferable permit' real but easy to check, so the permit component is a weaker moat than the power component.
- Ohio has 125+ data-center moratoriums (https://www.mahoningmatters.com/news/state/article317296239.html). That may ease competition for shells locally, but it also weakens the 'disappearing shells' urgency in Ohio.
result.sharper_angle:
Change who pays and drop the parts that are already crowded. Do not sell a scoring database to manufacturers, because LandGate, Enverus, Scout, Brownfield.ai and ZoomProspector cover parcel scoring and search. Sell an 'Electrical and Permit As-Built Record' to sellers and controllers of idle plants. That means bankruptcy trustees and liquidators, corporate real-estate divisions, county land banks, port and development authorities, and utility economic-development teams. They have a direct financial reason to prove a building's energized capacity, and the record supports a powered-shell premium.

1. Core deliverable: the electrician-verified one-line diagram, nameplates, gear age and condition, spare capacity, and a utility will-serve or capacity letter. Add slab and crane-rail condition and the state of the existing air and wastewater permits (shutdown status, fee and renewal compliance). Sell it as a standardised, dual-use record that both a manufacturer and a data-center, battery or powered-shell buyer can underwrite. The record then serves both buyer types instead of betting on the poorer one.
2. Channel: license the verified data as a white-label layer to AEP, FirstEnergy, JobsOhio and ZoomProspector-style databases. They list buildings but do not verify what is inside them.
3. Lead generation: use public Ohio EPA permit and parcel data to find idle plants and offer the seller a first record.
4. Drop the 0.5%-1% success fee. It likely needs a real-estate broker licence and creates conflicts with the seller-paid, buyer-trusted record. Charge per record and per data license instead.
5. Validate before building: get 5 sellers or liquidators to pre-pay for a record, and confirm that brokers or sellers will pay $1.5k-$3.5k. I found no evidence yet that they will.

competitors.name: Pew Research Center / NORC (public research on panel fraud)
competitors.what_they_do: Pew (Aug 2026) benchmarked opt-in sources against address-recruited panels. By trap questions, 18% of 11,114 respondents were bogus. Sentry flagged nearly half, and voter-file matching removed 64% of respondents and worsened bias. Its 2020 study found 4-7% bogus respondents in opt-in sources against about 1% in address-recruited panels. NORC published the fraud literature review (https://www.norc.org/content/dam/norc-org/pdf2026/cpss-research-brief-fraud-lit-review.pdf). The methodology is essentially the idea's 'address-recruited control comparison', published free and not sold as a per-study service.
competitors.scale_or_funding: Non-profit and academic research. Pew's American Trends Panel and NORC's panel are address-recruited and could be licensed as control samples (from background knowledge, not verified in this session).

result.white_space:
Detection is crowded and getting cheap: Verisoul, Roundtable, dtect, CloudResearch, Kantar Qubed, Research Defender, PureScore, ReDem and CleanID all sell it, some at cents per respondent. Cross-supplier scorecards already exist too, since Data Quality Co-op is a neutral clearinghouse. Building a detection ensemble or a generic vendor scorecard would be a fifth-to-tenth entrant against funded players.

What I did not find anyone selling:
1. A per-study ground-truth calibration. This means running a slice of the same questionnaire on a verified, address-recruited human control group and then reporting contamination-adjusted estimates with error bounds. Every vendor I found detects and removes. None quantifies how much bias survives the cleaning, and none re-estimates the result against a known-real reference. Pew's finding that voter-file matching removed valid respondents and made the error worse suggests 'remove the flagged' is itself a source of bias.
2. A neutral buyer-side referee that owns no sample. dtect is neutral but only sells entry-time detection. DQC is neutral but does not audit individual studies or supply a control sample. Verasight owns verified humans but sells sample.
3. Independent, third-party verification of the vendors' own accuracy claims. CloudResearch and Verisoul each claim 100% agent detection from internal or self-run tests. The Bot Olympics is MIT-judged but tests CloudResearch's own system.

The missing piece for a startup is the control panel. Building an address-recruited, device-attested panel of about 2,000 people is slow and expensive. The likelier route is to partner with or license an existing one (Verasight, NORC, Pew or Ipsos-style panels), not recruit from scratch.

This conclusion has limits. My WebSearch budget ran out at 200 calls, so I could not run the Crunchbase, YC or Product Hunt checks or search for a second wave of small startups. I also could not confirm funding for DQC, Roundtable, dtect or Verasight.
result.evidence_of_demand:
Problem demand is strong. Willingness to pay for a per-study, third-party audit is unproven, and I found no evidence of anyone paying $3-15k for one.

Problem evidence:
- Kantar reports post-field reconciliation (rejected sample) rates up about 300% in three years, with some clients rejecting up to 40% of data, and 89% of buyers naming data quality their top concern. This is a vendor source: https://www.kantar.com/inspiration/ai/is-panel-fraud-the-new-ad-fraud
- Pew (Aug 2026) found 18% bogus respondents in an 11,114-person opt-in test. Standard speeder and straightliner checks miss most of them: https://www.pewresearch.org/methods/2026/08/27/no-easy-fix-for-bogus-respondents-in-online-opt-in-polls/
- A 6,000-trial attention-check result for synthetic respondents (99.8% pass) and 15-30% panel fraud figures are cited in NORC and trade coverage: https://trends.vc/synthetic-audiences-verified-humans-panel-fraud-consent-gap/. CloudResearch's own test found 91.6% of AI agents passed all four traditional checks against 88.4% of humans: https://www.cloudresearch.com/resources/blog/ai-agent-detection/
- Trade press describes the problem as existential. Greenbook says fed-up research leaders are 'auditing suppliers, bringing sampling in-house and demanding accountability': https://www.greenbook.org/insights/tags/market-research-fraud. YouGov withdrew findings from a Bible Society survey after finding fraudulent respondents (via Obsurvant): https://www.obsurvant.com/news-and-data/ai-agents-survey-fraud-detection/

Spend on adjacent solutions:
- Buyers do pay for detection: Verisoul raised a $9M Series A, and EMI Research says post-survey removals fell from 30-40% to about 0. https://www.verisoul.ai/industries/market-research-survey-panels
- DQC sells a SaaS clearinghouse subscription, and CloudResearch says Sentry screens about 400M surveys a year.
- Emporia's buyer guide explicitly advises adding an independent third-party tool on critical studies because panel-owned tools carry a conflict: https://www.emporiaresearch.com/blog/a-buyers-guide-to-anti-fraud-tools-in-market-research-sampling

Counter-signals:
- Detection is priced at cents per respondent or $99-350 a month (Emporia's guide).
- Greenbook's 'Panel Quality Stinks and Clients Are To Blame' argues buyers will not pay more for quality, and it proposes no third-party audit: https://www.greenbook.org/insights/research-methodologies/panel-quality-stinks-and-clients-are-to-blame
- Touchstone's 'top 10 data quality companies' page lists no independent audit or ground-truth service: https://touchstoneresearch.com/market-research-data-quality-companies/. That supports the gap but comes from a vendor.
- I found no RFPs, regulations mandating audits, or public examples of audit fees.
result.sharper_angle:
Do not sell detection and do not build a generic vendor scorecard, since both are crowded. Sell independent bias quantification for decisions that will be challenged: a verified-human control sample plus a contamination-adjusted estimate with error bounds.

Buyers with a mandatory budget and an adversarial reader:
- Survey evidence in litigation and regulatory claim substantiation (Lanham Act, trademark and false-advertising surveys, FTC substantiation). Opposing experts attack panel quality here.
- Pharma quantitative studies used in market-access or pricing decisions.
- Polling publishers and journals that must defend their data.

Suggested shape:
- Partner or license the control panel from an existing address-recruited or verified panel (Verasight, NORC, Pew or Ipsos-style) instead of recruiting 2,000 people yourself.
- Ingest detection signals from dtect, DQC or Verisoul instead of building an ensemble.
- Own the neutral statistical layer: a replicated mini-questionnaire, a contamination-adjusted estimate, a bias-bound report and a signed audit letter.
- Publish a free, recurring 'state of sample quality' benchmark, the same design as Pew's study but across vendors and AI agents, as the marketing engine.
- Price per high-stakes study at $10-50k, not $3-15k. Expect low willingness to pay for routine studies, given that detection costs cents per complete.

Before building anything, validate the price with 5-10 insights heads and 2-3 litigation survey experts.

result.white_space: Provisional: I found no product or startup that mines a buyer's supplier invoices for tariff surcharge lines and pursues the supplier for a share of the IEEPA refund, on the buyer's behalf and for a contingency fee. The importer side is being served (TariffRefund.com self-serve, plus customs brokers and consultants). Freight and parcel audit vendors cover surcharge auditing. Generic AP recovery audit (PRGX) is the closest capability. What looks unserved is the buyer-as-claimant workflow: an automated surcharge ledger, supplier IEEPA-exposure estimates, contract pass-back language checks, claim letters, and CBP Form 4811 notify-party routing. It would target mid-market multi-unit franchisees, buying co-ops and GPOs, who are too small for PRGX-style enterprise engagements. The fuel-surcharge module is NOT white space because freight audit is a mature, crowded category. Caveat: my competitor scan is incomplete. The web-search budget was exhausted before any search ran, so this rests on direct page fetches of the CBP page, earnings transcripts and a handful of guessed vendor sites. Law-firm class actions or demand-letter campaigns, tariff-refund startups I could not surface, and customs brokers or couriers adding a pass-through service were not checked.
result.evidence_of_demand: Mixed. The underlying money and the pass-through gap are verified, but I found no direct evidence that downstream buyers are paying for a clawback service. (1) The refund flows only to the importer of record or its designated 4811 party, and CBP says nothing about downstream buyers: https://www.cbp.gov/trade/programs-administration/trade-remedies/ieepa-duty-refunds. (2) Windfalls are large and are being kept. AutoZone booked $96M in IEEPA refunds, and its CFO said the refund environment was deflationary, i.e. cost relief to retailers and suppliers rather than customer credits: https://www.fool.com/earnings/call-transcripts/2026/09/22/autozone-azo-q4-2026-earnings-call-transcript/. Cracker Barrel booked $15M ($9.1M net after reinvestment), with no mention of suppliers or pass-through: https://www.fool.com/earnings/call-transcripts/2026/09/23/cracker-barrel-cbrl-q4-2026-earnings-call-transcript/. MillerKnoll booked $16.5M (180 bps of gross margin), did not address refunds of customer surcharges, and announced a new 4% pricing action: https://www.fool.com/earnings/call-transcripts/2026/09/22/mlkn-q1-2027-earnings-call-transcript/. (3) Willingness to pay for importer-side help is shown by TariffRefund.com, which claims 330,000+ eligible importers with an average refund of about $503K (self-reported marketing): https://www.tariffrefund.com/. (4) Willingness to pay contingency-style recovery audits on supplier invoices is shown by PRGX's claimed $1.8B in annual recoveries: https://www.prgx.com. (5) Not found: forum complaints from buyers, RFPs, or buyer-side customers of any clawback service. Legal entitlement is also unproven, since a buyer who paid a price or surcharge often has no contractual right to the supplier's refund.
result.sharper_angle: Narrow to the claims that have a real legal hook and a buyer with leverage, and drop the fuel-surcharge module, which is a crowded freight-audit category. (1) Sell to buying groups, franchisee co-ops, GPOs and distribution co-ops as one negotiated, portfolio-level claim, not to individual franchisees. Leverage is collective, and their supply agreements often carry cost-plus, most-favored-customer, pass-through or 'refund if rescinded' clauses. (2) Screen every claim up front for an itemized tariff line or explicit pass-back language, and drive only those, jointly with a trade or commercial-litigation firm. The firm carries the legal risk and the product supplies the evidence: a clean surcharge ledger plus each supplier's estimated IEEPA exposure. This also makes the product a feed for plaintiffs' firms, which is a likelier revenue path than solo recovery. (3) Consider a supplier-side variant: a workflow that lets importers route refunds or credit memos to customers via 4811 and documents it. Large buyers will demand this in procurement, and suppliers want to keep goodwill without a dispute. (4) Move fast, because the window is roughly Q3-Q4 2026 and PRGX-type recovery-audit firms or TariffRefund.com could add a downstream module. Before building, re-run the competitor scan with working web search (tariff-refund pass-through startups, YC and Product Hunt, class actions and law-firm demand-letter campaigns, and customs brokers and couriers) and get a trade lawyer's view on whether buyers have any enforceable claim.

result.white_space:
Verified by fetches, with caveats below. No fetched page showed anyone selling a packaged, fixed-fee, design-stage (pre-tooling) HTS boundary audit for mid-market product brands ($10-100M revenue). None showed a bundled CBP binding-ruling filing with counsel review, or a ruling-watch product built on comparable-ruling analysis.

Software players (Zonos, Trademo, Descartes, Flexport) classify existing products. Tarifflo recovers past overpayments. Big-4 and law firms sell hourly advisory to large clients. A mid-market design-team buyer at the pre-tooling stage looks unserved.

Caveats that cap confidence:
1. The 200-call web search budget ran out before any search ran. Nothing was searched for boutique tariff-engineering consultancies, startups, YC or Crunchbase entries, Product Hunt, or open-source tools.
2. Several vendor fetches failed or returned thin pages: Altana, Avalara, Sandler Travis, Crowell, KPMG, Thomson Reuters, Expeditors and CROSS features.
3. So 'nobody does this exactly' is unproven. A specialist boutique or a well-funded new entrant may exist.

Structural risks that shrink the white space:
- Per 19 CFR 177.2, CBP rulings are limited to prospective transactions and require a full factual statement, samples and photos.
- Per 19 CFR 177.9, a ruling binds CBP only for the addressee and only for identical articles. Third parties cannot rely on it, and CBP can modify or revoke it without notice to anyone else.
- A classification ruling does not protect against Section 232 list changes. The lists are recalibrated and CBP treats sets by their primary classifying article. Redesigning across a line can be undone if the new line is later added to the list.
result.evidence_of_demand:
Weak to moderate, and mostly indirect. Direct customer pull for design-stage tariff engineering was not found. Some indirect signals:
1) Brands do tariff-engineer, and it is legal under a 'commercial reality' standard. Converse felt soles, Columbia nurse's pockets and Ford Transit Connect are the examples. The Ford case lost at the Supreme Court in 2020 because Ford removed the engineered features after import, which is a caution for the 'legitimately change the product' requirement. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tariff_engineering
2) Regulations force spend on product composition. Section 232 derivatives require reporting steel melt/pour and aluminum smelt/cast country of origin. Sets are dutied by their primary classifying article. https://www.cbp.gov/trade/programs-administration/entry-summary/232-tariffs-aluminum-and-steel-faqs. The fetched CBP page did not mention copper or the July 30, 2026 copper reporting claim, so that claim is unverified.
3) Mid-to-large importers pay for duty recovery. Tarifflo sells contingency audits to beauty, retail and manufacturing brands and claims 1 in 8 entries has errors, about $35.9B a year in overpayment. It benchmarks against $250-500/hour consultants. These are vendor claims, not independent data. https://www.tarifflo.com/
4) Large vendors sell duty mitigation and classification to shippers at every size, which shows budget exists. https://www.livingstonintl.com/, https://www.flexport.com/, https://www.trademo.com/
5) CBP frames rulings as a tool for 'business decisions that are dependent on how their goods will be treated on importation'. This is a capability, not demand. https://www.cbp.gov/trade/rulings

Not found, because search was unavailable: forum complaints, RFPs, buyer interviews, or evidence that mid-market brands pay $4.5-35k for this. The idea's own premise that importers avoid ruling requests is unverified.
result.sharper_angle:
Do not sell 'tariff engineering' as a generic service, because the big brokers, Big-4 and law firms could add it as a line item. Pick a defensible wedge instead.

1) One vertical, such as e-bike/powersports parts or bags and footwear. Build a structured database of CROSS rulings tagged by construction and material thresholds. That data becomes the moat, and a free 'boundary map' of a prospect's top SKU becomes the lead magnet.

2) Sell into the design and product-development stage gate, before tooling is cut. A fixed-fee 'pre-tooling tariff spec review' should be a standard step alongside costing and compliance. Price as a per-product-line retainer, not one-off audits.

3) Make the binding ruling an optional deliverable filed by a licensed broker or attorney partner, not by you. Work with brokers and trade law firms as the channel, since they hold the license and the client relationship.

4) Add a rate-scenario stress test to every redesign recommendation. A ruling protects the classification, not the rate. Section 232 lists and derivative rules keep changing, so each redesign should be scored on how likely the new line is to be swept into a future list. This directly answers the biggest weakness in the current pitch.

5) Avoid success-fee pricing on savings until counsel is comfortable. Redesign must survive the 'commercial reality' test, so document that each change is permanent and serves a real manufacturing or commercial purpose.

Before building anything, redo the search work that was skipped here. Search for boutique tariff-engineering consultancies, Crunchbase, YC and Product Hunt entries, and how Flexport, Livingston and the Big-4 price duty-mitigation work. Then run 10 buyer interviews at $10-100M brands to test whether product teams would pay at the design stage."

result.white_space:
Caveat on process: the session's WebSearch budget was exhausted (200 of 200) before I could run any search. I researched only by fetching about 20 known URLs directly and by using prior knowledge. "No scaled startup found" therefore means not found, not verified absent. Rerun 6-8 searches (Crunchbase, YC, Product Hunt, 'shared aide' and 'cluster care' startup terms) before committing capital.

What looks unserved: (1) A private-pay, tiered, per-building shared-aide subscription in market-rate or workforce 55+ apartment buildings that are not part of a campus. Existing players are either nonprofit coordinator programs (SASH, Selfhelp, NCR), Medicaid or state-licensed programs (PACE, NJ-style ALP), or campus operators (Brookdale). I found no venture-scale company selling this. (2) A dispatch and acuity-tiering software layer for in-building routing (floors, elevators, overnight response). Nothing I fetched showed one.

Serious risks that shrink the white space:
- Licensing. Under Minnesota 144G.08, sleeping accommodations plus any 'assisted living services' (personal care, toileting help, medication reminders, meal setup, safety checks) under contract requires an assisted-living license. Subsidized housing is excluded unless marketed as assisted living, and the statute does not address a property owner that arranges a home-care provider on site. 'Assisted-living-without-the-license' is therefore legally fragile in many states, especially with an owner revenue share and overnight response, which look like 'holding out'.
- Unit economics. Two aides per shift is 17,520 aide-hours a year, about $400-500k loaded at roughly $23-28 an hour. Spread over 15 residents at $2,200 a month ($396k a year) that is break-even at best. At 6-10 residents the cost per resident is about $4,000-5,000 a month, which is above the stated $1,800-3,500 tiers. The idea's own numbers are internally inconsistent (6-10 residents in the one-liner, 15 in the pilot).
- Substitutes. BAYADA and franchise agencies already market to senior-living partners, and NCR and Brookdale could add pods in-house.
result.evidence_of_demand:
Verified in this session:
- Price anchor matches the idea. CareScout's 2025 national median is $35 an hour for a non-medical caregiver ($80,080 a year at 44 hours a week) and $6,200 a month for assisted living ($74,400 a year). https://www.carescout.com/cost-of-care
- Affordability gap. NIC's site highlights a Health Affairs study that more than half of middle-income seniors will lack the financial resources for senior housing and care by 2029, and reports half of primary markets above 90% occupancy. https://www.nic.org/ (headline-level only, and I could not open the Health Affairs paper: 403).
- Buyers and payers already fund on-site models. SASH has 5,300+ participants at 200+ Vermont sites, https://sashvt.org/. Selfhelp reports $3,937 in Medicaid savings per resident and 68% lower hospitalization odds across 19 buildings, https://www.selfhelp.net/. NCR serves 75,000+ seniors a year and pairs housing with home health aide services, http://www.nationalchurchresidences.org/. PACE has 97,000+ participants, https://www.npaonline.org/.
- Regulatory context. Minnesota's statute shows states treat this bundle as assisted living: https://www.revisor.mn.gov/statutes/cite/144G.08

Not found: any price-point evidence for $1,800-3,500 shared-aide tiers, any owner RFPs for it, or resident complaints about in-building care gaps. From prior knowledge only: assisted-living occupancy near 90%, low construction starts, the 2026 visa pause and Medicaid HCBS waitlists (the idea's own claims), none re-verified.
result.sharper_angle:
Do not lead with 'assisted living without the license' or a 24/7 two-aide pod. Both carry the largest licensing risk and the worst unit economics.

Narrower version: an overnight-response and transfer/toileting 'night pod' plus scheduled ADL rounds, sold as a contracted, resident-billed home-care service (a licensed agency subcontracted per state), not as a property amenity. The building owner provides only space and a call system, with no revenue share and no marketing as care, which avoids 'holding out' triggers like Minnesota's.

Pick launch states where the structure is clear, for example states with an explicit assisted-living-in-subsidized-housing or shared-care Medicaid pathway. Then use market-rate 55+ buildings to prove the private-pay density economics before touching Medicaid.

Build the software as the moat: acuity-tier dispatch, in-building routing, and aide-minutes-per-resident data. That data proves move-out avoidance to owners and can be sold as a managed-service or white-label layer to agencies like BAYADA and to nonprofit owners like NCR, instead of running aides yourself.

Fix the math first. Model at least 12-15 residents per two-aide overnight pod, price at $2,800-3,500 a month, and confirm the per-state labor and licensing rules before the 90-day pilot.

result.white_space:
Caveat: the WebSearch budget (200 of 200) was exhausted before I could run any queries, so this verdict rests on direct page fetches of known companies. It is not a broad sweep. I could not run forum, Reddit, WhatsApp-group, RFP, Spanish/Portuguese-language or Crunchbase/YC/Product Hunt searches. My 'nobody does cross-company mining pooling' finding is therefore unconfirmed and moderate-confidence.

STEP ONE (SAP dedupe and surplus cleaner) is crowded and should not be the business. Verusen has a live mining case study ($96.8M identified across 17 sites), a listing in the SAP Store, about $33M disclosed funding and enterprise references. SPARETECH does the same dedupe-and-surplus job. Partium and Syniti cover the normalization and SAP-cleansing pieces. The 'LLM cost collapsed, so now it's viable' argument is weak, because Verusen and SPARETECH already do this. The remaining wedge inside step one is small: mid-size mines (roughly $30-150M of spares, one SAP instance, no enterprise budget) below Verusen's Fortune-100 and multi-site-enterprise focus, sold on a success fee. That is a thin, copyable wedge.

STEP TWO (neutral, cross-operator critical-spares pool) is unserved among the players I checked. Verusen's sharing module is intra-company only and has no legal, insurance or inspection layer. Liquidity Services and RB Global sell surplus one-way and offer no loan or lease terms. Grid Assurance proves the pooled long-lead-spares subscription model for utilities, but nobody I found has applied it to mines. The unserved piece is the trust wrapper: a neutral entity, standard loan/lease agreement, third-party condition certification (vibration/NDT), logistics and insurance, and a single-point-of-failure spares register per district.

Risks I could not close out. (1) OEM reman, exchange and consignment programs (haul-truck components, mill liners, motors) are the real substitute for pooling. I could not verify their current terms because the Cat Reman fetch timed out. (2) Competition-law exposure when competing operators share inventory data needs early legal work. (3) The pooled-event frequency is low, so revenue per district is modest, and pooling in Chile or Peru needs local counsel. (4) Verusen could add an inter-company network cheaply; it already lists 'Spare Parts Sharing' and mining customers.
result.evidence_of_demand: Demand for step one (paying for dedupe and surplus identification) is well evidenced, which is also why it is crowded. Verusen's mining case study reports $96.8M of identified inventory value across 17 sites (https://verusen.com/use_case/use-case-global-mining-enterprise/). Verusen claims about $20M working capital unlocked per customer within 12 months and 10x ROI (https://verusen.com). It raised $25M in a Series B in Jan 2022 (https://verusen.com/news/announcing-verusens-25m-series-b-funding/). SPARETECH claims about 20% average inventory reduction (https://www.sparetech.io). A pulp-and-paper customer of Verusen reports $10M saved directly from parts sharing across its own sites, so sharing itself has proven value inside one company (https://verusen.com/blog/how-hub-and-spoke-inventory-sharing-cuts-mro-costs-across-sites-without-risking-downtime/). Utilities already pay for a pooled long-lead spares subscription (Grid Assurance, https://www.gridassurance.com). Corporations already route surplus through marketplaces such as Liquidity Services, which reports $15B+ in completed sales (https://www.liquidityservices.com/). I found NO direct evidence that mining operators pay for cross-company pooling: no forum threads, RFPs, or documentation of the claimed WhatsApp swap networks (search budget was exhausted). Treat the 'informal swap network' premise and the '20-30% duplicates' figure as founder assertions to test in discovery calls.
result.sharper_angle: Drop the standalone SAP-cleaner wedge, because Verusen (mining case study, SAP Store listing, about $33M funding) and SPARETECH already own it. Build only the neutral cross-operator layer, modelled on Grid Assurance's utility pool but for mines. Form a district co-op or SPV with 3-5 neighbouring mid-size operators (for example Arizona/Nevada or Antofagasta first) and start with a register of only the 15-30 single-point-of-failure spares with 12-24 month lead times: mill drive motors, girth gear and pinion sets, main transformers, SAG/ball mill shells. Sell it as a restoration-assurance subscription that bundles a pre-signed standard loan/lease agreement, third-party condition certification (vibration, NDT), pre-agreed mobilization logistics and insurance. Price it on membership plus a per-event fee, not a share of freed cash. Use a minimal anonymized matching step (OEM part number and serial for critical items only, taken from a CSV export) as the free on-ramp, or partner with or resell Verusen/SPARETECH for the cleanup so you never compete with them. Position it as the inter-company layer Verusen does not offer. Before writing any software, validate three things. First, whether OEM consignment and reman programs already cover most of the risk. Second, competition-law clearance. Third, whether 3 signed operators will put one real spare into the pool. The bare 'success fee on freed cash' product is not defensible.

result.white_space:
The idea's core claim is that Main Street firms have 'nobody to appraise or sell their data'. That is now false in general. Sellmybusinessdata.com, Troveo and FileYield all pitch AI-buyer data sales to manufacturing, logistics and insurance firms. SimpleClosure's asset report names the same verticals. What I found nobody doing:

(1) Closure-event channel. No one is embedded in the workflows of business brokers, CPAs, liquidators, ABC assignees and Chapter 7/Subchapter V trustees who handle non-VC small-business closures. Those advisors have a fiduciary or client-service reason to surface an overlooked estate asset. The competitors are direct-to-seller or startup-founder-led.

(2) Time-critical capture. The data is destroyed when the QuickBooks/ERP/email/TMS subscriptions lapse and owners retire. A closure-triggered preservation and rights-clearing workflow is different from a generic 'sell your data' page.

(3) Vertical-specific packaging. Examples are freight-broker quote/dispatch/TMS logs or machine-shop RFQ, quote and work-order sets matched to named buyers building vertical agents. The competitors are horizontal.

(4) Insolvency-grade rights review for non-consumer-PII operational data. The competitors' rights and de-identification work is generic and consumer-PII-adjacent.

The proposed pricing is a weakness. A 25-35% fee plus a $500-1,500 scan competes against $0 upfront (Sellmybusinessdata), 0% seller fee (Troveo) and 8% (FileYield). Reported startup archive deals run $10K-$100K, so 30% of a small machine shop's corpus may not cover rights-review and packaging costs.
result.evidence_of_demand:

1. No funded company sells human-executed, ad hoc, arbitrary-protocol wet-lab work through an agent-native ticket API with a fixed price and a signed record separating AI proposal, human edit and physical execution. The nearest pieces are split across companies. Adaptyv has the agent API but runs standardized automated assays. CRO marketplaces have custom human work but run on quotes and SOWs. Transfyr has the execution-record capture but no labor. Emerald and Ginkgo have flexible automation but were not found to offer human-run ad hoc work to agents.
2. The long tail beyond fixed assays is the actual gap. That means multi-step, protocol-specific molecular biology that a robot cannot be programmed for in time: novel enzyme or nuclease activity validation, cloning plus cell-free expression plus a custom activity readout, and unusual cell-culture assays. Anthropic's post confirms this is where a frontier lab keeps human scientists.
3. Nobody I found sells biosafety-screened human execution of AI-proposed protocols as a service, even though oversight of AI-directed experiments is in the news (Lab Manager, 'Biosafety Oversight for AI-Directed Lab Experiments', Sept 28, 2026; Frontiers paper on automated-lab security tiers).

The window is narrow and closing.
- Adaptyv has $40M, agent-native positioning, a stated plan to add 'more complex biological workflows', and Chai and Boltz as customers. It can move toward the ad hoc tail with automation.
- Scientist.com and Science Exchange could add an agent API or MCP layer around their existing providers with modest effort.
- Transfyr could bundle records with any CRO.
- Anthropic and other frontier labs are insourcing bench capacity.

Risks to the idea's own claims:
- BioSpace headlines show layoffs are easing: August 2026 biopharma layoffs were about 500, down 90% year over year, and the Q2 job report says postings are rising. Skilled hands are still available, but the 'layoff wave' supply story is weakening (via https://news.google.com/rss/search?q=biotech+layoffs+2026+BioSpace+job+cuts+tracker).
- Sublet-bench operations carry insurance, contamination, quality-control and IP-chain-of-custody risk that a software-style API hides.
- The 35-45% gross margin at $1.5-8k per experiment is unproven against commodity CROs and against Adaptyv's automation, which starts at $149 per protein for screening-level binding.

Demand for agent-orderable wet-lab validation is real. Demand for human-run ad hoc work, specifically as a paid service to agents, is plausible but not directly evidenced.

Evidence that AI-first teams pay for outsourced physical validation:
- Adaptyv raised a $40M Series A in Aug 2026. It has 100+ customers including AI-native labs Chai Discovery and Boltz plus Roche and Novo Nordisk, throughput is up 5x in a year, and it is tripling capacity. Its own stated endpoint is 'enough automated experimental capacity for AI to learn from physical reality as quickly as it learns from text' (https://www.startupticker.ch/en/news/adaptyv-raises-40m-to-build-automated-lab-for-agentic-biology; https://www.adaptyvbio.com/blog).
- Adaptyv ships an MCP server so Claude can order experiments (https://docs.adaptyvbio.com/llms.txt). Anthropic and Adaptyv launched a protein-design competition with 5,000+ experimental validations (Dealroom, Sept 22, 2026).
- Ginkgo lists 130+ customers for cloud lab and Datapoints services (https://www.ginkgo.bio/). OpenAI's GPT-5 ran 36,000 experiments in Ginkgo's cloud lab, and Ginkgo staff still handled reagents and consumables (https://www.rdworldonline.com/ginkgo-co-founder-reshma-shetty-on-autonomous-labs-ai-designed-experiments-and-the-human-side-of-the-equation/).
- Scientist.com cites $3B+ of scientific procurement activity and 6,000+ providers (https://www.scientist.com). This is existing spend on outsourced custom bench work.
- Benchling launched one-click ordering with Twist, Adaptyv and Ginkgo (PR Newswire, May 6, 2026).
- Funding is flowing into AI-lab infrastructure: Transfyr $25M seed, Medra $52M Series A, Lila and Periodic at multi-billion-dollar valuations (Google News RSS results).

Evidence that human bench work is the bottleneck the idea targets:
- Anthropic's Sept 2026 post says 'All of the lab work is performed by human scientists'. It says automation 'is less conducive to the sort of ad hoc workflows that are involved in our molecular biology research'. It also says 'If you have a proposal for a research question, we would like to hear from you' (https://www.anthropic.com/news/claude-discovers-novel-enzyme-system).
- The Stanford Virtual Biotech (37,000 agents) coverage is dated Sept 17-19, 2026. A Korea JoongAng Daily headline on Sept 22 reads 'AI drug race moves from finding candidates to proving they work'.
- OpenAI Foundation's Public Data for Health program gave $125M for biology data generation (Inside Precision Medicine and MIT Technology Review, Sept 15, 2026). That is grant-funded demand for data generation, though not specifically for outsourced human bench work.

Evidence gaps: I found no forum complaint, RFP or paying-customer example specifically for human-executed ad hoc experiments ordered by agents. I found no evidence of regulation forcing spend on execution records; Lab Manager's Sept 28 piece on biosafety oversight suggests the topic is emerging. The demand evidence is therefore mostly for adjacent, automated or CRO-based services.
result.sharper_angle:
Do not build a general 'bench-for-hire API'. That collides with Adaptyv, which has $40M, an MCP server and a stated move into complex workflows, and with CRO marketplaces that could add an API in a quarter. Build the overflow and escalation tier that automated and catalog vendors cannot serve, and sell it with biosafety and provenance attached.

1. Narrow the scope to agent-discovered novel proteins, meaning enzymes, nucleases, reverse transcriptases and CRISPR-like systems, where the work is cloning plus cell-free or cell expression plus a bespoke activity readout. Robots do not have these protocols pre-programmed, and Anthropic's own post says it keeps humans at the bench for exactly this. Sell it first to AI-for-protein and agent-swarm startups, and to frontier-lab science teams that would rather subcontract than build more bench capacity.
2. Make the differentiator a human-executed, biosafety-screened, attested record. Each ticket gets a biosafety review of the AI-proposed protocol by a senior scientist. It returns a signed record separating AI proposal, human edit and physical execution, with raw data. This targets the unaddressed oversight gap (Lab Manager, Sept 28, 2026) and is something Adaptyv's automation-only positioning does not sell. It also gives frontier labs a compliance reason to route work to you.
3. Partner rather than compete on fixed assays. Route standard binding, expression and thermostability to Adaptyv or Ginkgo through their APIs and take only the tickets they reject or cannot express. Integrate with Transfyr-style capture instead of building sensors. That removes the commodity margin fight and turns the biggest competitors into a lead source.
4. Cut the sublet-bench plan. Start inside one or two existing CRO or shared labs (an incubator such as LabCentral or a partner CRO) with insurance, contamination control and IP chain of custody already in place. Use the laid-off scientists as a vetted contractor bench, but treat layoffs as a recruiting channel, not a growth thesis, since layoffs are easing.
5. Validate demand before building. Get 3 paid pilots from AI-protein startups and one frontier-lab science team at $1.5-8k per ticket, and test whether they pay a premium for the biosafety and provenance record. Anthropic's public invitation for outside research proposals is the first outreach target. If nobody pays a premium over what Adaptyv or a CRO charges, the idea collapses into a low-margin CRO and should be dropped.

Verdict basis: the digital-regulation half of the idea (GDPR Art. 27 + AI Act + Data Act + NIS2 + DSA) is already served by at least three established providers, each with a multi-regulation catalog. Prighter has a live bundle discount and EDPO has flat all-inclusive packages. Four things remain unserved or weakly served.

1. Hardware and connected-product makers. The privacy and digital reps (Prighter, EDPO, DataRep) do not appear to offer GPSR, CRA or sector product-safety representation, and the product-side rep (Obelis) does not appear to offer GDPR, AI Act, Data Act or CRA. Nobody I found sells both halves. The buyer is a non-EU IoT, consumer-electronics or industrial-AI company that needs GPSR responsible person, Data Act representative, GDPR Art. 27, CRA and AI Act Art. 22 at once. This is the only wedge that survives.

2. Genuinely substantive, liability-bearing representation. AI Act Art. 22 obliges the rep to verify the declaration of conformity and technical documentation, hold documents for 10 years and terminate the mandate if the provider breaches. Art. 54 gives the GPAI rep a similar duty over Annex XI documentation. Vendors such as EDPO explicitly disclaim internal compliance and act as a liaison. A rep that actually reviews the technical file (an 'AI Act notified-body-lite' role) is a different, higher-priced product that I did not find anyone offering at scale.

3. Execution gaps. DataRep's AI Act and Data Act pages still say 'finalising our service', and none of the vendors publish a shared cross-regulation register of representations, SLA-backed triage, or unified invoicing beyond a discount.

4. Timing. CRA vulnerability and incident reporting applies from 11 Sep 2026 (EC page: https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/policies/cyber-resilience-act), with main obligations from 11 Dec 2027. The CRA authorised representative is optional and narrow, so it is a weak demand driver.

Roll-up thesis weaknesses. (a) Market price points are far below the idea's EUR 3-15k per bundle: about EUR 420-4,750 per year per service at Prighter, and from EUR 150 at DataRep, with 40% bundle discounts. (b) The AI Act rep TAM is small: only non-EU GPAI providers and non-EU high-risk providers, and open-source GPAI is exempt under Art. 54(6) unless it poses systemic risk. (c) GDPR Art. 27 representation is largely a commodity postbox, so 'someone who can be sued' commands little premium in that segment. (d) I found no evidence of small rep shops being for sale at 1-2x revenue, and Prighter, EDPO and DataRep are natural competing acquirers.

result.white_space:
I found no scrap, recycling or transfer-station-specific acquisition accelerator. Every searcher or ETA program I could verify is sector-agnostic, and none packages this asset class for a first-time buyer. That is limited evidence. The session's 200-call WebSearch budget was already spent. I fell back on Google News RSS, the Hacker News API, the Federal Register API and direct fetches, and could not reach Crunchbase, Product Hunt, Reddit, Searchfunder or BizBuySell.

What looks unserved:
1. A vertical diligence and financing pack for sub-$5M scrap and recycling yards. It would cover Phase I/II and fire-history checks, insurance, permit transferability and offtake contracts. Horizontal ETA programs leave that to each buyer. Fire and insurance risk is live: EMR's Camden yard was shut after 15 fires in six years (NJ PEN, 29 May 2026), Resource Recycling wrote 'Battery fire risk isn't going away. Insurance is responding' (24 Feb 2026), and a 9,000-car Idaho salvage yard burned (Yahoo, 19 Jun 2026).
2. A succession desk for owner-run yards. Nothing I found targets ReMA-type family operators with a packaged successor, and the big consolidators only want larger yards.
3. A permit-and-owner-age target list. Nothing I found offers one for scrap dealers.

The premise needs two corrections:
- The BIS rule is real. It is a temporary final rule, published 6 Aug 2026 and effective 27 Aug 2026. However, it covers only black mass and tungsten waste and scrap, not ordinary ferrous or nonferrous yards (Federal Register 2026-16078). The 'domestic scrap re-rating' story is much narrower than the pitch implies.
- The idea leans on 'laid-off managers with $100-300K'. That is a crowded buyer-education market, with Codie Sanchez, Kingsway and the universities all courting the same buyers.

result.sharper_angle:
Drop the laid-off-generalist tuition play and become the scrap and recycling succession and diligence desk.

1. Sell to retiring owners and lenders first. Build the permit- and owner-age-based target list and a 'sale-ready yard' package: pre-run Phase I, fire and insurance file, permit-transfer memo and offtake summary. Charge owners a listing or readiness fee, and license the diligence pack to SBA lenders. Keep the cohort as a lead source, not the main revenue line.
2. Partner instead of competing on buyer education. Offer the vertical module to Search Fund Accelerator, Kingsway-style programs, university ETA clubs and Codie Sanchez-type communities. Recruit buyers with industrial operations backgrounds, not laid-off tech managers, because the operational and safety risk is the hard part.
3. Consider a small holdco or operators-in-residence model in the Kingsway style, with your capital taking the equity, so revenue does not depend on $4-6K tuitions. Target yards at $1-5M revenue, below the size where Sims, Radius and Tenaris bid.
4. Use the BIS rule only where it applies. The specific unserved niche is small owner-run tungsten-carbide and hard-metal scrap dealers, and possibly black mass aggregators, which the DPAS allocation order covers. Avoid auto salvage and ITAD, where PE is already active.
5. Make fire and insurance underwriting the differentiator. Most first-time buyers cannot underwrite it, and it is the risk that kills yards.

Before building, check three things I could not: whether ReMA or a scrap M&A broker already offers a successor-matching service, whether Codie Sanchez's programs cover scrap yards, and whether SBA lenders will actually lend against contaminated yards.
